citations.narrative:
Approximately 4-6 pig enclosures previously used and currently unoccupied guinea pig enclosures containing old bedding
and left ove animal urine and fecal waste had not been cleaned out. This used bedding and leftover waste contributed to
the strong ammonia odor within the facility. The licensee must ensure that all used bedding, food and animal waste are
disposed of in a timely manner to minimize pests, disease hazards and odors that can affect the guinea pig's respiratory
system and overall health.

An enclosure with two guinea pigs had a build up of organic matter along the interior walls of the enclosure with
approximately 10 small gnats flying around. This build up of organic matter can contribute to odors, disease, and pest
attraction. This build up must also be removed to allow for sanitization. Licensee must ensure that the primary enclosure
is cleaned often enough to prevent accumulations that can cause odors, attract pests or cause disease to the animals.

Approximately 10-20 small flies and gnats were seen to annoy two guinea pigs (flinching and constantly moving) in their
enclosure on a wooden shelving unit located above the tortoise enclosure. A full fly strip was present as were two, 2-liter
bottles with fly attractant that were half full. The licensee must ensure the pest control program is effective and maintained
to prevent pests, stress to the animals, disease hazards, and contamination of food and bedding.

Within the facility (housing guinea pigs, rabbits, ferrets, chinchillas, hedgehog, a bird and feeder rats/mice) there were 4-6
empty enclosures (containing used bedding and animal waste) that had not been cleaned out. The used bedding and
leftover waste are contributing to the strong ammonia odor within the facility. Licensee must ensure that all used bedding,
food and animal waste are disposed of in a timely manner to minimize pests, disease hazards and odors that can affect
the rabbit's respiratory system and overall health.

The facility does not have a provision for the disposal of animal and food wastes, dead animals and trash. The small,
shed-sized facility houses 42 regulated animals plus additional unregulated animals (tortoise, rats, feeder mice and rats)
and other husbandry items. Wet, soiled bedding shows urine/excreta that are being produced by a variety and number of
animals (chinchilla, rabbit, gerbil, ferret, guinea pig, hedgehog, and a bird), and feeder- animals that are housed (stacked
on shelves next to each other) within the same area of the facility producing an irritating odor to the inspector. The
ammonia odor was most intense near the door (middle of the facility) and a stacking of feeder rats. Food waste from the
tortoise, along with 4-6 previously used, empty enclosures with soiled bedding (containing urine/fecal waste) present on
the shelves (from the previous week) also contributed to the ammonia odor and acted as a pest attractant (small flies and
gnats) that were seen to annoy the guinea pigs. Improper disposal of animal and food wastes and bedding can cause
high levels of ammonia and other odors that can create health diseases and hazards for the animals and attract flies and
other pests. Licensee must ensure that the disposal methods in the facility shall be so provided and operated as to
minimize vermin infestation, odors, and disease hazards..
